beats.title: Lesson 17 — Hardening the OpenPLC Login
beats.sub: Closing the door we walked through
beats.say: Welcome back to CybICS. We now switch to defence. In lesson five we walked in through a weak OpenP L C login. In this lesson we close that door, and harden the credentials.

beats.head: The weakness: a default account
beats.body:
OpenPLC ships with a built-in default account, openplc / openplc. Default credentials are one of the most common ways into ICS.
  • The fix is simple but essential: change the password (keep the username).
  • The CybICS dashboard verifies it by checking that the default login no longer works.
  • This is a D3FEND credential-hardening control.
beats.say: OpenP L C ships with a built in default account, user name openplc, password openplc. Default and shared credentials are one of the most common ways into an industrial system. The fix is simple but essential: change the password, while keeping the account. And the dashboard verifies our work by checking that the default login no longer works.

beats.caption: Confirm the weakness: the default login still works
beats.cmd: curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'openplc/openplc login -> HTTP %{http_code}   (302 = the default password still works!)\n' -X POST -d 'username=openplc&password=openplc' http://172.18.0.3:8080/login
beats.say: First we confirm the problem. We try the default credentials against the login, and the server answers with a redirect, three zero two. The default account is live. Anyone who knows it is already inside.

beats.caption: Harden it: change the default password, then re-test
beats.cmd: J=/tmp/def; curl -s -c $J -b $J -X POST -d 'username=admin&password=ramirez' http://172.18.0.3:8080/login -o /dev/null; curl -s -c $J -b $J -X POST http://172.18.0.3:8080/edit-user -d 'user_id=10' -d 'full_name=OpenPLC User' -d 'user_name=openplc' -d 'user_email=openplc@cybics.local' -d 'user_password=S3cure-ICS-2026!' -o /dev/null -w 'change password -> HTTP %{http_code}\n'; curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'openplc/openplc login -> HTTP %{http_code}   (200 = blocked, the default is dead)\n' -X POST -d 'username=openplc&password=openplc' http://172.18.0.3:8080/login
beats.say: Now we harden it. As an administrator we open the user settings and set a strong, unique password on that account, keeping the username the same. Then we re-test the default. This time the server returns the login page, two hundred. The default credentials are dead. In a real deployment you would do this in the OpenP L C web interface, under Settings and Users.

beats.head: Verify the defense
beats.body: The CybICS dashboard runs the same check we just did: it tries the default credentials and confirms they are rejected. We open the challenge and let it verify our work.
beats.say: The CybICS dashboard runs exactly the same check we just did, trying the default credentials and confirming they are now rejected. We open the challenge on the dashboard and let it verify our defence.

beats.caption: Verify the defense in the CybICS dashboard - on the attack machine
beats.say: On the dashboard we open the harden OpenP L C credentials challenge and click verify defence. The check runs, the default login is confirmed disabled, and the challenge is marked solved.

beats.head: What we learned
beats.body:
• Change every default and shared credential before a device goes live.
  • Use strong, unique passwords, and remove accounts you do not need.
  • Where the device supports it, add lockout and multi-factor; where it does not, isolate the interface.
beats.say: To recap: change every default and shared credential before a device goes live, use strong unique passwords, and remove the accounts you do not need. Where the device supports it, add account lockout and multi factor authentication, and where it does not, keep the interface off any network an attacker can reach.
